BUSS1020 Week 12

BUSS1020 Week 12 — Regression Inference, Diagnostics and Multiple Predictors

Regression notation

For simple regression, Yᵢ = β₀ + β₁Xᵢ + εᵢ and the fitted line is ŷᵢ = b₀ + b₁xᵢ. Observation i has predictor xᵢ, response yᵢ, fitted response ŷᵢ and residual eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ. The population intercept and slope are β₀ and β₁; b₀ and b₁ are their sample estimates. The unobserved population error is εᵢ. A sample of n observations has means x̄ and ȳ. Define SSX = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², where Σ means summation over observations.

The residual standard error, also called SER or sₑ, is √[SSE/(n − 2)] in simple regression, where SSE = Σeᵢ². It estimates the standard deviation of errors in response units. It is distinct from a coefficient's standard error, which measures sampling uncertainty in that coefficient estimate.

L.I.N.E. assumptions

Linearity: the population conditional mean has the stated linear form, E(Y|X) = β₀ + β₁X. The vertical bar means “conditional on”.

Independence: errors from different observations are independent under the classical model. Sampling design, time ordering and clustering matter.

Normality: the errors conditional on predictors are normal for exact classical small-sample inference and the usual individual prediction interval.

Equal variance: Var(ε|X) = σ² is constant across predictor values. This is homoscedasticity; unequal conditional variance is heteroscedasticity.

Ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates coefficients by minimising the sum of squared residuals; this calculation does not require normality. Large samples can support approximate coefficient inference under suitable regularity conditions, but n > 30 alone is not a universal justification. The Central Limit Theorem concerns sampling distributions of suitable statistics; it does not make raw responses or individual errors normal. Even n = 500 does not imply normally distributed errors. Individual prediction intervals require assumptions about individual errors, not just a nearly normal coefficient estimator.

Testing coefficients and constructing intervals

In a model with k predictors excluding the intercept, test H₀: βⱼ = βⱼ,₀ using:

t = (bⱼ − βⱼ,₀)/SE(bⱼ), with df = n − k − 1.

j identifies the coefficient, βⱼ,₀ its hypothesised value, and SE(bⱼ) its estimated standard error. For a zero null, the numerator is bⱼ. Use the coefficient standard error from the fitted model, not the predictor's standard deviation.

A two-sided 1 − α interval is:

bⱼ ± t*SE(bⱼ),

where t* is the positive 1 − α/2 percentile with the same residual degrees of freedom and α is the significance level. Reject a matching two-sided null if its value is outside the interval, or if the two-sided p-value is below α. For a two-sided critical-value decision, compare |t| with t*.

In simple regression, k = 1, df = n − 2 and:

SE(b₁) = sₑ/√SSX.

This shortcut does not generally hold for an individual slope in multiple regression when predictors are correlated. A nonsignificant intercept does not prove that the population intercept is zero or justify automatically forcing the fitted line through the origin.

For simple regression, the overall zero-slope F statistic equals the square of the slope t statistic: F = t². Its p-value equals the two-sided zero-slope t p-value. In multiple regression, the overall F test and each individual t test do not have this general equivalence.

Testing a zero population correlation

Let ρ denote population correlation and r sample correlation. Under the classical conditions for this test:

H₀: ρ = 0 against H₁: ρ ≠ 0 uses t = r√[(n − 2)/(1 − r²)], with df = n − 2.

This is equivalent to the zero-slope test in simple regression. For an intercept model, r = sign(b₁)√R², where sign(b₁) supplies the slope's positive or negative sign and R² is the fraction of observed response variation explained by the model. The displayed test formula is specific to a zero correlation null; substituting an arbitrary nonzero ρ₀ into its numerator does not create a valid general test.

Zero correlation means no linear association. It does not establish independence or exclude nonlinear relationships. Excel's Multiple R is nonnegative and equals |r| in simple regression.

Mean-response confidence interval and individual prediction interval

At a predictor value x₀ within the relevant observed range, the fitted value is ŷ₀ = b₀ + b₁x₀. Define:

h₀ = 1/n + (x₀ − x̄)²/SSX.

Target

Two-sided interval

Population mean response E(Y

X = x₀)

One new response Y₀ at X = x₀

ŷ₀ ± t*sₑ√(1 + h₀)

Here t* is the 1 − α/2 t percentile with n − 2 degrees of freedom. Both intervals have the same centre and nominal confidence level. The prediction interval is wider because it includes both uncertainty about the estimated mean and the new individual's error, represented by the additional 1. Both widths are smallest at x̄ and grow as x₀ moves away from x̄.

These are simple-regression formulas. They are not a general replacement for multiple-regression leverage calculations. Classical individual prediction intervals depend on conditional normal errors and an appropriate variance model. The ability to substitute a number outside the observed range does not make extrapolation reliable.

Residual diagnostics

A scatterplot and domain knowledge help select a plausible relationship. After fitting, inspect residuals before relying on tests, confidence intervals or predictions.

• Residuals against fitted values or X: a random horizontal band around zero supports the mean form and constant variance. Curvature suggests a missing nonlinear pattern; a fan-shaped spread suggests heteroscedasticity.

• Residuals against time or order: runs, waves or systematic sequences suggest dependence. A pattern-free fitted-value plot alone cannot establish independence; cross-sectional data may also be dependent.

• Normal Q–Q plot: approximately linear alignment supports normality. Systematic curvature indicates departures. A roughly bell-shaped histogram and skewness and excess kurtosis near zero are supporting diagnostics, not proof.

• Standardised residuals: dividing every residual by the same positive residual scale changes units but preserves patterns. Leverage-adjusted or studentised residuals instead use observation-specific scales and should be distinguished from this common-scale construction.

• Potential outliers: |standardised residual| > 3 is a flag for investigation, not an automatic deletion rule. A normal model can itself generate extreme observations.

Constructing a residual Q–Q plot in Excel

For each residual, let aᵢ be its ascending rank, using average ranks for ties:

RANK.AVG(residual,locked_range,1) gives aᵢ.

Calculate plotting position qᵢ = (aᵢ − 0.5)/n.

Calculate theoretical normal score zᵢ = NORM.S.INV(qᵢ).

Plot residuals vertically against theoretical z scores horizontally.

The half-rank offset avoids probabilities of zero and one. It is a plotting-position convention, not a binomial continuity correction. Approximate linearity, rather than a nonlinear Q–Q pattern, supports a normal-error approximation.

Worked examples

Example 1 — House-price slope and correlation

For ten houses with price measured in thousands of dollars and area in square feet, the estimated slope is b₁ = 0.1097677 and SE(b₁) = 0.03296944. To test H₀: β₁ = 0 against β₁ ≠ 0:

t = 0.1097677/0.03296944 ≈ 3.329.

Residual df = 10 − 2 = 8. At 5%, t* = 2.3060, so reject because 3.329 > 2.3060. The two-sided p-value is 0.01039. The matching slope interval is:

0.1097677 ± 2.3060(0.03296944) ≈ 0.03374 to 0.18580 thousand dollars per square foot,

or approximately $33.74 to $185.80 per additional square foot, rounded in coefficient units to (0.0337,0.1858). This estimates a population mean-price association, not a guaranteed price increment for each house.

The zero-correlation test produces the same t. Squaring gives t² ≈ 11.08, matching overall F = 11.0848 up to rounding.

Example 2 — Intervals for a 2000-square-foot house

The ten-house data are (area in square feet, price in $1000):

(1400,245), (1600,312), (1700,279), (1875,308), (1100,199), (1550,219), (2350,405), (2450,324), (1425,319), (1700,255).

They give x̄ = 1715, SSX = 1,571,500, fitted equation ŷ = 98.24833 + 0.1097677x, and sₑ = 41.33032. At x₀ = 2000:

ŷ₀ = 98.24833 + 0.1097677(2000) = 317.78381.

h₀ = 1/10 + (2000 − 1715)²/1,571,500 = 0.1516863.

With df = 8, the 95% critical magnitude is 2.306004.

Mean-response margin = 2.306004 × 41.33032 × √0.1516863 ≈ 37.1195.

Mean-response interval = 280.6643 to 354.9033, approximately 280.66 to 354.90.

Individual prediction margin = 2.306004 × 41.33032 × √1.1516863 ≈ 102.2812.

Individual prediction interval = 215.5026 to 420.0650, approximately 215.50 to 420.07.

All prices and limits are in thousands of dollars. The first interval estimates the mean price of houses of this area; the second predicts the price of one new house. Neither is the slope interval. The area 2000 lies inside the observed 1100–2450-square-foot range.

Example 3 — Sunflowers Apparel coefficient intervals

For 14 stores, the fitted annual sales model in millions of dollars is ŷ = −1.209 + 2.074 × Customers, with Customers measured in millions. The slope standard error is approximately 0.254. With df = 12, a 95% t critical magnitude is about 2.179:

2.074 ± 2.179(0.254) ≈ 2.074 ± 0.5535.

Using the unrounded fitted quantities, the slope interval is 1.522 to 2.627. It excludes zero and indicates a positive conditional mean association. The intercept interval is −3.376 to 0.959, which includes zero. It does not establish that the intercept is exactly zero. Rounding the displayed coefficient and standard error before calculation can slightly change the last reported digits.

Example 4 — Weight model with seven predictors

A multiple-regression model for response weight has n = 812, k = 7 predictors and residual df 812 − 7 − 1 = 804. Binary gender coding uses female = 1 and male = 0. The overall model p-value is approximately 8.8 × 10⁻⁶⁵, providing strong evidence that at least one population slope is nonzero.

An individually nonsignificant predictor named International may be considered for removal followed by refitting and reassessment, but deleting every nonsignificant predictor is not a universal modelling rule. Variable selection must consider the question, domain knowledge and diagnostics. A fan-shaped residual plot raises concern about unequal variance; deleting a predictor does not automatically remedy it. Reassess the resulting fitted model rather than assuming a change has fixed the variance pattern.

Autocorrelation and the Durbin–Watson statistic

Autocorrelation is dependence between errors across time or another meaningful order. For ordered residuals e₁,…,eₙ, the Durbin–Watson statistic is:

D = Σᵢ₌₂ⁿ(eᵢ − eᵢ₋₁)² / Σᵢ₌₁ⁿeᵢ², provided the denominator is nonzero.

The numerator measures consecutive changes; the denominator measures overall residual magnitude. D lies between 0 and 4. Values near 2 are consistent with little first-order autocorrelation; lower values suggest positive autocorrelation and higher values suggest negative autocorrelation. These are diagnostic tendencies, not universal significance cutoffs or proof of independence at every lag.

A bounds decision requires lower and upper critical bounds dL and dU matched to n, k excluding the intercept, significance level and testing convention:

Statistic range

Interpretation under an appropriate bounds procedure

D < dL

Evidence of positive first-order autocorrelation

dL ≤ D ≤ dU

Inconclusive

dU < D < 4 − dU

Fail to reject the relevant no-first-order-autocorrelation null

4 − dU ≤ D ≤ 4 − dL

Inconclusive

D > 4 − dL

Evidence of negative first-order autocorrelation

The middle region does not prove independence. One-sided and two-sided conventions require appropriately calibrated bounds, and these rules are not universally applicable to arbitrary designs or models with lagged dependent variables. A time-order residual graph diagnoses model behaviour; it is not itself a forecasting model.

Multiple regression and adjusted R²

With k predictors, the population and fitted models are:

Yᵢ = β₀ + Σⱼ₌₁ᵏβⱼXⱼᵢ + εᵢ,

ŷᵢ = b₀ + Σⱼ₌₁ᵏbⱼxⱼᵢ.

j indexes predictors, i indexes observations, and k excludes the intercept. Each slope describes the predicted mean-response change associated with a one-unit change in its predictor holding all other included predictors constant. It is not necessarily the predictor's unconditional pairwise association with Y.

For an intercept model, SST = Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)², SSE = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)², and R² = 1 − SSE/SST. Adjusted R² is:

1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k − 1),

or equivalently 1 − [SSE/(n − k − 1)]/[SST/(n − 1)].

Compare appropriate models using the same response and observations. Ordinary R² cannot fall when adding predictors to a nested intercept OLS model; adjusted R² can rise or fall because it penalises use of residual degrees of freedom. It can be negative and is not an ordinary percentage explained.

The overall F = [SSR/k]/[SSE/(n − k − 1)], where SSR = SST − SSE, has df (k,n − k − 1) under the classical null. It tests whether all population slopes are zero against at least one nonzero slope. Individual coefficient t tests have df n − k − 1; a significant overall F does not imply that every individual coefficient is significant.

Example A — Weekly pie sales

The model is:

Predicted pies per week = 306.526 − 24.975 × Price + 74.131 × Advertising.

Price is dollars per pie; Advertising is measured in $100 units. For Price = $5.50 and advertising expenditure $350, enter 5.5 and 3.5:

306.526 − 24.975(5.5) + 74.131(3.5)

= 306.526 − 137.3625 + 259.4585

= 428.622, approximately 428.62 pies per week.

Holding advertising fixed, a $1 price increase is associated with 24.975 fewer predicted pies per week. Holding price fixed, an extra $100 in advertising is associated with 74.131 more predicted pies. These are model associations rather than guaranteed intervention effects.

Categorical predictors and dummy variables

For m mutually exclusive categories in an intercept model, use m − 1 binary indicators. Each indicator equals 1 for its category and 0 otherwise. The omitted category is the reference group. Including all m indicators with an intercept creates exact redundancy; using arbitrary labels such as 0,1,2 as one continuous predictor imposes an unjustified numerical spacing instead.

A dummy coefficient estimates a conditional-mean difference from the reference group while other predictors are held fixed. With no interactions, category-specific lines have different intercepts but the same numerical-predictor slope: they are parallel. Four seasons therefore require three indicators with one season, such as Winter, as reference.

Example B — Holiday indicator

ŷ = 300 − 30 × Price + 15 × Holiday, where Holiday = 1 for a holiday week and 0 otherwise.

For non-holiday weeks, ŷ = 300 − 30 × Price. For holiday weeks, ŷ = 315 − 30 × Price. Both slopes are −30; at the same price, predicted holiday-week sales are 15 units higher.

Example C — Three housing categories

Take colonial homes as the reference. Define Dranch = 1 for ranch homes and 0 otherwise, and Dsplit = 1 for split-level homes and 0 otherwise:

The fitted response is ŷ = 20.43 + 0.045 × Area + 23.53 × Dranch + 18.84 × Dsplit.

• Colonial: ŷ = 20.43 + 0.045 × Area.

• Ranch: ŷ = (20.43 + 23.53) + 0.045 × Area = 43.96 + 0.045 × Area.

• Split-level: ŷ = (20.43 + 18.84) + 0.045 × Area = 39.27 + 0.045 × Area.

At a fixed area, the predicted ranch response is 23.53 response units above colonial and the split-level response is 18.84 units above colonial. All categories share a slope of 0.045 response units per area unit. Without specified measurement units, these coefficients should remain in model units rather than being assigned invented dollar or floor-area scales.

Excel inference functions

• T.DIST.2T(ABS(t),df) calculates a two-sided coefficient-test p-value.

• T.INV.2T(alpha,df) gives the positive two-sided critical magnitude; it takes the full α, not α/2.

• F.INV(1-alpha,k,n-k-1) returns the upper-tail overall-F critical value.

• Regression output gives coefficient standard errors, two-sided p-values and coefficient intervals. Confidence levels other than 95% can be specified.

• Multiple-regression inference uses the reported model-specific coefficient standard errors rather than the simple-regression shortcut.
